draft.title: Irony and satire
card: a gap between what is said or expected and what is meant or what actually happens. A writer who calls a leaking, rusty bucket a "fine ship" is using irony.
Verbal irony is when words mean something different from what they say. Situational irony is when events turn out very differently from what we expect.
writing that uses irony and humour to criticise people or society. It may exaggerate a flaw so that readers see it clearly.
Irony makes readers notice the gap and work out the real meaning. In satire, this can make a reader laugh and also question the thing being criticised.
draft.remember: Irony is a gap between what seems true and what is meant. Satire uses that gap, with humour, to criticise.

opts: It uses irony and humour to criticise people or society
It uses humour only to make readers laugh
It states a writer's opinion in plain, serious words
It describes events that turn out as expected
a.why: Satire uses irony and humour for a purpose: to criticise. Humour alone is not enough, because a text that only entertains is not satire.
a.clue: Satire has a target, not just a joke.

b.q: A town council spends a fortune on a new sign reading "Our town saves money". Then it cuts the library's opening hours. A columnist praises the council for its "brilliant thrift" and for "bravely protecting the sign budget". What is the columnist doing?
opts: Using irony and humour to criticise the council
Using plain, serious words to praise the council
Using situational irony to describe an accident
Using humour only to entertain readers
b.why: The columnist says "brilliant" and "bravely" but means the opposite, which is verbal irony. Combined with humour, it is aimed at criticising the council, so it is satire. Praise on the surface does not mean the columnist is really praising.
b.clue: Do the words match what the writer really thinks?

a.best: It uses irony and humour to criticise people or society

b.best: Using irony and humour to criticise the council
